introduction: The people of the Bayán were the followers of the Báb, and these readings, most of them from Bahá’u’lláh, address those among them who did not accept him as the one the Báb had promised, many of whom followed Mírzá Yaḥyá instead. The language is that of a wounded appeal and a severe rebuke, written during exile and under attack from former companions. The quotations beside them show how old the pattern is, in the prophets, the Gospels and the Qur’an, where a people who hold a scripture do not receive the one it promised. Because the readings give one side of a division whose other side still has heirs, a larger share than usual is set in contrast or complement: the tests a community may rightly apply to a claim, the warnings of Jesus, Paul and the Qur’an against deriding and cursing, and Mill's reminder to hear the other side.
questions: What exactly are the people of the Bayán charged with in these readings: disbelief, pride, calumny, or violence? Which charges could a reader today weigh, and how?
Deuteronomy, Paul and Jesus each tell believers to test new claims. How do the readings distinguish testing from denial?
Bahá’u’lláh writes that he would make peace with them: if they will not love him, let them not hate him. What does that sentence add to the rebukes around it?
How should strong words written under persecution be read by people who were not there, on the Qur’an's counsel not to deride or revile?
What do the readings ask of those who did recognize, lest they repeat the pattern?

outside.why: John's Gospel opens on the same sorrow: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Jesus tells his critics that Moses, in whom they trust, is the one who accuses them, for Moses wrote of him.
Acts praises the Bereans for receiving the word with readiness and searching the scriptures daily to see whether it was so.
Paul tells the Galatians to hold accursed even an angel from heaven who preaches another gospel than the one received. How is faithfulness to what was given told from blindness to what comes next?
Deuteronomy gives Israel a test for one who speaks in the name of the Lord. By what tests may a community rightly weigh a new claim without being counted among the deniers?
Abraham in the parable says that those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded though one rose from the dead.
Isaiah is sent to a people who hear indeed and understand not, who see indeed and perceive not.
Jesus thanks the Father that these things are hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed unto babes.
Elijah tells God that the children of Israel have forsaken the covenant, and I, even I only, am left.
Milton's seraph Abdiel is found faithful among the faithless, and holds his ground alone.
The psalmist saw the wicked spreading like a green bay tree, and he passed away and was not.
Gamaliel advises leaving a new movement alone: if it be of men it will come to nought, and if of God it cannot be overthrown. Does his counsel bind both parties to a schism?
Paul lists what he bore for his message: thrice beaten with rods, once stoned.
Stephen asks his judges which of the prophets their fathers did not persecute.
The Qur’an forbids one folk to deride another, who may be better than they. How should a reader today hear a whole community called the most ignorant of peoples?
Proverbs says that he who is first in his own cause seems just, until his neighbour comes and searches him. Where can a reader hear the other party's own account?
Paul warns the branches grafted in not to boast against those broken off. What does the pride charged against one community ask of the community that follows it?
Jesus warns of false Christs and false prophets who show great signs. Each side of such a dispute reads the warning as aimed at the other: how is a seeker to judge?
The Qur’an tells believers to argue with the people of earlier scripture only in the better way.
Jesus asks his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who despitefully use them.
Jesus charges the teachers of his day with laying aside the commandment of God to hold the tradition of men.
Isaiah pronounces woe on those who put darkness for light and light for darkness.
The Qur’an offers its own verses as proof and challenges doubters to produce a chapter like them.
Hebrews uses the figure of milk for those unskilful in the word, not yet weaned to strong meat.
Jesus asks why we behold the mote in a brother's eye and not the beam in our own. What does the saying ask of anyone who repeats a sweeping judgment on another community?
John records that though Jesus had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him.
Santayana warned that those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
The Qur’an says that most follow nothing but conjecture, and conjecture can by no means take the place of truth.
The psalmist is compassed about with words of hatred and a lying tongue: for my love they are my adversaries.
Mill warns that he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that. These letters give one side of a bitter division: what would hearing the other require?
Jesus laments over Jerusalem, how often he would have gathered her children, and they would not.
Jesus says in his own town that no prophet is accepted in his own country.
Paul's counsel is to live peaceably with all men, if it be possible, as much as lieth in you.
A short chapter of the Qur’an ends a dispute without hatred: unto you your religion, and unto me my religion.
The Qur’an tells Muhammad that messengers were denied before him, and were patient under the denial.
The psalmist could have borne it from an enemy, but it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide and mine acquaintance.
Zechariah has one asked about the wounds in his hands answer that he was wounded in the house of his friends.
Jesus ends a parable with the saying that many are called, but few are chosen.
The Qur’an speaks of those who awaited a scripture confirming their own, and disbelieved when it came.
Tennyson finds more faith in honest doubt than in half the creeds. Is every doubter heedless, or may doubt be an honest stage on the way?
Jesus weeps over the city that did not know, in its own day, the things which belong unto its peace.
Some in the crowd reject Jesus because the Christ, they have read, cannot come out of Galilee.
Isaiah asks who has believed our report, and to whom the arm of the Lord is revealed.
The Qur’an says they would put out the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect his light.
James says that blessing and cursing ought not to proceed out of the same mouth. How is a reader to hold a curse in scripture and this counsel together?
When disciples wish to call down fire on a village that would not receive him, Jesus rebukes them. What separates a judgment pronounced by God from a believer's wish to see it fall?
Ezekiel is told to call the breath from the four winds upon the slain, that they may live.
Jesus says his doctrine is not his own but his that sent him, the claim of one voice with one who came before.
The Qur’an commands that hatred of a people must not move believers to deal unjustly. How should strong words written under persecution be read by those who were not there?
In the parable the husbandmen beat and kill the servants sent to receive the fruit of the vineyard.
The Preacher says the thing that hath been is that which shall be, and there is no new thing under the sun.
Jesus tells his disciples that if the world hates them, it hated him before it hated them.
The Qur’an consoles Muhammad that it is not he they deny, but the revelations of God that they flout.
When Jesus heals a blind and dumb man, the Pharisees say he does it by the prince of devils.
The Qur’an records what was said of Muhammad in secret counsel: ye follow but a man bewitched.
Burke confesses that his countrymen cherish their old prejudices, and cherish them because they are prejudices. Is every inherited expectation a vain imagining?
Plato's prisoners in the cave have taken shadows for the truth all their lives.
The Qur’an records the answer given to every messenger: we follow that wherein we found our fathers.
Hearers of Jesus ask how this man knows letters, having never learned, and he answers that his doctrine is not his own.
The risen Lord of John's vision stands at the door and knocks, waiting for any who hear his voice.
Peter recalls that Christ, when he was reviled, reviled not again, and when he suffered, threatened not.
Micah laments a time when a man's enemies are the men of his own house.
Jesus gives the foundation the reading misses: love one another, as I have loved you.
Paul asks that one overtaken in a fault be restored in the spirit of meekness. Was there, and is there, a way back across this division?
The Preacher says that in the multitude of dreams and many words there are divers vanities.
The psalmist says the Lord is on his side: I will not fear, what can man do unto me?
Shakespeare has it that he who filches a good name takes what does not enrich him and makes the loser poor indeed.
The Qur’an says, follow not that whereof thou hast no knowledge, for hearing, sight and heart will be asked.
Jesus speaks of those who say that had they lived in their fathers' days they would not have shed the prophets' blood.
Jesus calls blessed the eyes that see and the ears that hear what many prophets desired.
Paul speaks of a veil that remains upon the heart when the old scripture is read.
The psalmist's own familiar friend, in whom he trusted, who ate of his bread, has lifted up his heel against him.
Paul asks whether God has cast away his people who did not accept, and answers, God forbid. Does a community that refuses a new revelation fall outside God's care?
Jesus tells his disciples he has many things to say, but they cannot bear them now.
Jesus asks Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
In the parable the servants would gather up the tares at once, and are told to let both grow until harvest. Who is fit to name the satans in a community?
Paul is troubled on every side yet not distressed, perplexed but not in despair.
Jesus quotes the psalm: the stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner.
Jesus says that the love of many shall wax cold, but he that endures to the end shall be saved.
Jesus tells Simon that he has prayed for him, that his faith fail not.
Jesus walks beside two of his own, and their eyes are holden that they should not know him.
Joseph's brothers, seeing their father love him more, hated him and could not speak peaceably unto him.
Lincoln took up the saying that a house divided against itself cannot stand.
Kant calls tutelage self-incurred when it lies in want of courage to use one's own reason.
The neighbours of Jesus were offended at him because they knew his trade and his family.
Antony says that Brutus, whom Caesar loved, gave the most unkindest cut, and ingratitude quite vanquished him.
Jesus compares those who hear and do not act to a man who built his house upon the sand.
Paul's charge is to watch, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men and be strong.
The father of the prodigal sees his son a great way off, runs and falls on his neck.
Jesus tells John not to forbid one who does not follow with them, for he that is not against us is for us. Can blessing reach those of the Bayan who stayed where they were?
The psalm says that they who trust in the Lord shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed.
Jesus warns of false prophets in sheep's clothing who inwardly are ravening wolves. Each party to a schism applies the figure to the other: what settles it?
Jesus says of certain teachers that they are blind leaders of the blind, and both shall fall into the ditch.
The Pharisees ask whether any of the rulers have believed, as though that settled it.
Elijah asks the people how long they will halt between two opinions.
John's letter tells believers not to believe every spirit but to try the spirits, whether they are of God.
Jesus likens outward piety to whited sepulchres, beautiful without and full of dead men's bones within.
Jesus asks what it profits a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
Jesus prays for those who crucify him: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. Is there room beside this rebuke for that prayer?
The Qur’an tells believers not to revile what others pray to, lest they revile God in ignorance. How should those who study these rebukes speak of the people they name?

zechariah-wounded-in-the-house-of-my-fri.text: And one shall say unto him, What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends

matthew-stone-which-the-builders-rejecte.text: Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes

james-blessing-and-cursing.text: Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be

micah-enemies-of-his-own-house.text: For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house

john-though-he-had-done-so-many-miracles.text: But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him

luke-neither-will-they-be-persuaded.text: And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead

genesis-hated-him-and-could-not-speak-pe.text: And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him

quran-they-deny-not-thee.text: We know well how their talk grieveth thee, though in truth they deny not thee (Muhammad) but evil-doers flout the revelations of Allah.

quran-unto-you-your-religion.text: Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion.
